title: Saint Mary Magdalene (22 July)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saints Peter and Paul, Petros, the fisherman and the tentmaker. Your line was two pillars. Whom did you thank? Day six hundred seventy-six.

Mary Magdalene, the repentant prostitute: that's the woman in a great many paintings, films and sermons, going back centuries. Here's the problem. The Gospels never say it. Not once. What they do say about her is far more interesting, and in 2016 the Church did something about it. Pope Francis raised her day, the twenty-second of July, from a memorial to a feast, the same rank as the apostles. And the Vatican's decree gave her an old title: apostle of the apostles.
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE THINK THEY KNOW.` → `THE GOSPELS NEVER SAY IT.` → `2016: RAISED TO A FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Gospels actually say. Luke names her among the women who traveled with Jesus and supported his work from their own means, and says seven devils had gone out of her: some serious affliction, healed. Matthew, Mark and John name her at the cross, after the other disciples had scattered. And all four put her at the empty tomb on Easter morning. In John she's alone in the garden, weeping, and mistakes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says one word: her name, Mary. Then he sends her. Go to my brethren. And John says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Mary Magdalen cometh, and telleth the disciples: I have seen the Lord, and these things he said to me." In John, the first person sent to announce the resurrection is a woman, and the people she's sent to are the apostles. That's where the title comes from: apostle means one who is sent. So where did the other story come from? In 591, in a homily, Pope Gregory the Great treated Mary Magdalene, the unnamed sinful woman who anoints Jesus in Luke, and Mary of Bethany as one person. That reading shaped Western art and preaching for centuries. The Eastern churches kept them as three women. After the Second Vatican Council, the Roman calendar quietly separated them again, and the Gospel for her day became the garden in John. Thomas Aquinas, long before, had already called her apostolorum apostola. The Church's own feast now tells her story the way the Gospels do.
screen: `HEALED, AND A FOLLOWER.` · `AT THE CROSS, AT THE TOMB.` · `SENT: I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.` · `GREGORY'S MERGER, AND ITS UNDOING.` · then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry good news. Sit, and think back over the last week. Find one piece of genuinely good news, yours or someone else's: a recovery, a kindness, a baby, a reconciliation, a small win. Hold it for a moment and let yourself feel it. Then decide who needs to hear it, and how you'll tell them today. If you pray, you can give thanks for it first. The bell holds the time.
apostolorum apostola. Latin for apostle of the apostles, the old title for Mary Magdalene, sent first from the garden to announce the resurrection. Today's word.
Your line: she was sent. Today, tell the good news you found to the person who needs it, before the day is out. Day six hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on 22 July, raised from a memorial in 2016; the Gospel at Mass is John's account of her meeting the risen Jesus in the garden and being sent to the disciples.
